contents.html: 7.1 RETHINKING ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT AUTHENTICATION
contents.html_ja: 7.1 認証に関する前提の再考
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p86: 見出し 7.1

contents.html: The findings from this study illustrate how often knowledge workers authenticate during a typical day, that the impact from those events can linger beyond the enabling task of authentication, and that coping mechanisms are employed to reduce that impact. These findings suggest that it is necessary for security professions to acknowledge and respect the limits of users. When users’ cognitive limits are reached; they resort to variety of memory aids, some of which may have unintended security implications.
contents.html_ja: この調査の結果は、ナレッジワーカーが典型的な 1 日にどのくらいの頻度で認証するか、それらのイベントの影響が認証という実現タスクを超えて尾を引く可能性があること、そしてその影響を減らすために対処の仕組みが用いられていることを示しています。これらの結果は、セキュリティ専門家がユーザーの限界を認識し、尊重する必要があることを示唆しています。ユーザーの認知的限界に達したとき、ユーザーはさまざまな記憶補助手段に頼ります。その一部は、意図しないセキュリティ上の影響をもたらす可能性があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p86: 段落と一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: 「認証という認証を可能にするタスク」の重複を資料内の訳語「実現タスク」で直す。

contents.html: 7.1.1 Users struggle with authentication because they are only human
contents.html_ja: 7.1.1 ユーザーが認証に苦労するのは、人間にすぎないからである
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p86: 見出し 7.1.1

contents.html: Security specialists may be under the impression that users fail to practice good security behaviors because they are completely unaware of the consequences of their actions, or because they do not care about organizational security. This is not typically the case. Most users are aware, in principle, that they have a responsibility to help maintain organizational security. They also understand that part of that responsibility involves fulfilling authentication requirements. The authentication diary study participants were certainly aware of this, and took the importance of organizational security very seriously.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティの専門家は、ユーザーが良いセキュリティ行動をとらないのは、自分の行動の結果をまったく認識していないか、組織のセキュリティを気にかけていないからだと思い込んでいるかもしれません。これは、通常は当てはまりません。ほとんどのユーザーは、原則として、組織のセキュリティの維持に協力する責任があることを認識しています。また、その責任の一部が、認証要件を満たすことを含むことも理解しています。認証の日誌調査の参加者は、確かにこれを認識しており、組織のセキュリティの重要性を非常に真剣に受け止めていました。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p86: 段落と一致

contents.html: However, on a practical, day-to-day basis, users’ principal objective is to accomplish their primary tasks. Authentication makes that more difficult than it would otherwise be, because it disrupts users’ workflow (especially if it is complex, time-consuming, and/or prone to problems). The time-and-effort costs of authentication and the disruption it causes – which are both compounded by the number, type, and success or failure of authentication events – accumulate across tasks and applications over time.
contents.html_ja: しかし、実際の日々の現場では、ユーザーの主たる目的は、主要タスクを達成することです。認証は、ユーザーのワークフローを中断させるため（特に、複雑で、時間がかかり、問題が起きやすい場合）、それを本来よりも困難にします。認証の時間と労力のコストと、それが引き起こす中断は、どちらも認証イベントの数、種類、成功または失敗によって増幅され、時間とともにタスクとアプリケーションをまたいで蓄積します。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 段落と一致

contents.html: Therefore, users lose sight of the value of security measures as their attention naturally gravitates to the immediate task of meeting authentication requirements as quickly and efficiently as possible (which is the reason for coping mechanisms). When users encounter authentication, they tend to see it as a hassle first and a necessity second. This is not because users are stupid, malicious, or lazy; they are simply having an instinctive human reaction to being interrupted and detoured on the way to accomplishing their goals [17].
contents.html_ja: したがって、ユーザーの注意は、認証要件をできるだけ早く効率的に満たすという目前のタスクに自然に引きつけられます（これが対処の仕組みの理由です）。そのため、ユーザーはセキュリティ対策の価値を見失います。ユーザーは認証に遭遇すると、まず面倒なものと捉え、次に必要なものと認識する傾向があります。これは、ユーザーが愚か、悪意がある、あるいは怠惰だからではありません。目標の達成に向かう途中で中断され、回り道をさせられることに対する、人間としての本能的な反応を示しているにすぎません [17]。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.1.2 More authentication is not necessarily better
contents.html_ja: 7.1.2 認証が多いほど良いとは限らない
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 見出し 7.1.2

contents.html: Some of the study participants admitted that certain authentication coping mechanisms they used – such as writing passwords down, or using the same password for multiple accounts – had the potential to compromise organizational security. But without these coping mechanisms, it is difficult to use and manage many passwords. What choice did they have?
contents.html_ja: 一部の調査参加者は、パスワードを書き留める、複数のアカウントで同じパスワードを使うなど、自分たちが使っていた特定の認証への対処の仕組みが、組織のセキュリティを損なう可能性があることを認めました。しかし、これらの対処の仕組みがなければ、多くのパスワードを使用し管理することは困難です。彼らにどのような選択肢があったでしょうか。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 段落と一致

contents.html: In security design, making the user authenticate for everything is often the path of least resistance. But taking that path adds significantly, and possibly unnecessarily, to a user’s authentication burden.
contents.html_ja: セキュリティ設計では、あらゆるものについてユーザーに認証させることが、最も抵抗の少ない道であることがよくあります。しかし、その道をたどることは、ユーザーの認証の負担を大幅に、そしておそらく不必要に増やします。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.2 MAKING PASSWORD-BASED AUTHENTICATION MORE USABLE
contents.html_ja: 7.2 パスワードベースの認証をより使いやすくする
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 見出し 7.2

contents.html: Making authentication more usable is, ultimately, a long-term prospect. It will require not only a major shift in perspective, but extensive research and development efforts: we suggest some possible directions for both in Sec. 7.3. Fortunately there are steps that organizations can take in the relatively short term to reduce their users’ authentication burden.
contents.html_ja: 認証をより使いやすくすることは、結局のところ、長期的な見通しです。それには、視点の大きな転換だけでなく、広範な研究開発の取り組みが必要です。両方について、考えられる方向性を第 7.3 節で提案します。幸いなことに、組織が比較的短期間で、ユーザーの認証の負担を減らすためにとれる措置があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.2.1 Listen to and work with users
contents.html_ja: 7.2.1 ユーザーの声を聞き、ユーザーと協力する
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87: 見出し 7.2.1

contents.html: Making users more aware of and educated about the importance of organizational security and authentication’s role in it can help increase users’ compliance budgets [5]. Users will be more tolerant of authentication and other security policies and measures if they feel they understand the rationale behind them. The participants in this study were probably more accepting of authentication than they otherwise would have been because NIST makes it a point to foster a culture of security awareness, in no small part through relevant education and training. However, such measures will not give users an inexhaustible compliance budget [5]. Even the most patient and security-positive users have limits.
contents.html_ja: 組織のセキュリティの重要性と、その中での認証の役割について、ユーザーの認識を高め、教育することは、ユーザーのコンプライアンス予算を増やす助けとなりえます [5]。ユーザーは、認証やその他のセキュリティポリシーと対策の背後にある根拠を理解していると感じれば、それらに対してより寛容になります。この調査の参加者は、NIST が、関連する教育と研修を通じて、セキュリティ意識の文化を醸成することに力を入れているため、そうでない場合よりも認証を受け入れていた可能性が高いです。ただし、そのような措置が、ユーザーに無尽蔵のコンプライアンス予算を与えるわけではありません [5]。最も忍耐強く、セキュリティに前向きなユーザーにも、限界があります。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p87〜88: ページをまたぐ段落で全文を確認

contents.html: For users juggling many authentication elements, resorting to coping mechanisms – such as writing passwords down, reusing them, caching them in browsers, or employing management tools – is a rational way to reduce the impacts of authentication on their primary tasks. But from the point of view of organizational IT and security personnel, these coping strategies can shift user behavior into unintended territory. In this reactive posture, IT ends up lagging somewhat behind user workarounds that have not been assessed for risk or compliance, a situation that may create security vulnerabilities of which users are unaware.
contents.html_ja: 多くの認証要素をやりくりしているユーザーにとって、パスワードを書き留める、再利用する、ブラウザにキャッシュする、管理ツールを使うなどの対処の仕組みに頼ることは、認証が主要タスクに与える影響を減らす合理的な方法です。しかし、組織の IT およびセキュリティ担当者の視点からは、これらの対処戦略は、ユーザーの行動を意図しない領域へと移す可能性があります。この受け身の姿勢では、IT は、リスクやコンプライアンスの評価を受けていないユーザーの回避策に、いくらか遅れをとることになり、これはユーザーが気づいていないセキュリティ上の脆弱性を生み出しうる状況です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 段落と一致

contents.html: Organizational IT and security personnel need to support their users in this area. This means engaging users in discussions about authentication, encouraging them to share their friction points and coping mechanisms – and then following up with constructive action. Soliciting feedback from users and addressing their problems should be part of the organization’s iterative security process. Robust organizational security depends upon the willing and active cooperation of users.
contents.html_ja: 組織の IT およびセキュリティ担当者は、この領域でユーザーを支援する必要があります。これは、ユーザーを認証についての議論に参加させ、摩擦点と対処の仕組みを共有するよう奨励し、その後、建設的な行動で対応することを意味します。ユーザーからのフィードバックを求め、その問題に対処することは、組織の反復的なセキュリティプロセスの一部であるべきです。堅牢な組織のセキュリティは、ユーザーの自発的で積極的な協力に依存します。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.2.2 Implement SSO
contents.html_ja: 7.2.2 SSO を実装する
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 見出し 7.2.2

contents.html: Many of the study participants expressed a desire for NIST to implement organization-wide SSO. They said they would accept a password that is longer and more complex than any they are currently required to use, so long as it was the only one they had to use. Indeed, government employees in a much larger study regarding attitudes towards passwords expressed a preference for SSO [5].
contents.html_ja: 多くの調査参加者は、NIST が組織全体の SSO を実装することを望んでいると表明しました。彼らは、使用しなければならないパスワードが 1 つだけであるなら、現在使用を求められているどのパスワードよりも長く複雑なパスワードを受け入れると述べました。実際、パスワードに対する態度に関するはるかに大規模な調査で、政府職員は SSO への選好を表明しました [5]。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 段落と一致

contents.html: SSO would solve many of the pressing usability problems described by our participants, such as having to manage multiple complex passwords with different composition rules and expiration schedules. While SSO may be difficult and expensive to implement for an organization, it may be a worthwhile investment, since it would significantly cut down on authentication-related friction and disruption and their subsequent costs.
contents.html_ja: SSO は、異なる構成規則と有効期限のスケジュールを持つ複数の複雑なパスワードを管理しなければならないことなど、参加者が述べた差し迫ったユーザビリティの問題の多くを解決するでしょう。SSO は、組織にとって実装が困難で費用がかかるかもしれませんが、認証に関連する摩擦と中断、およびそれに続くコストを大幅に削減するため、価値のある投資かもしれません。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.2.3 Consolidate and standardize authentication as much as possible
contents.html_ja: 7.2.3 認証を可能な限り統合し標準化する
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88: 見出し 7.2.3

contents.html: If it is not feasible for an organization to implement actual SSO, the best alternative is to meet users halfway and implement a uniform password policy. Even if the policy chosen for universal application is the one with the most stringent content rules and the shortest expiration time, it will still help users by reducing the confusion and inconsistency that makes it more difficult for them to cope with their authentication workloads. If an overhaul of existing password policies is considered to be too difficult and disruptive, the organization should at least dictate that all future applications and systems that use password-based authentication should have the same policy.
contents.html_ja: 組織が実際の SSO を実装することが実現可能でない場合、最善の代替策は、ユーザーに歩み寄って、統一されたパスワードポリシーを実装することです。全体に適用するために選ばれたポリシーが、最も厳格な内容規則と最も短い有効期限を持つものであっても、ユーザーが認証の作業負荷に対処することをより困難にしている混乱と不整合を減らすことで、ユーザーの助けになります。既存のパスワードポリシーの全面的な見直しが、あまりにも困難で混乱を招くとみなされる場合、組織は少なくとも、パスワードベースの認証を使用する今後のすべてのアプリケーションとシステムが、同じポリシーを持つべきだと定めるべきです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p88〜89: ページをまたぐ段落で全文を確認

contents.html: The lack of a uniform, consistent password policy made it that much harder for participants to create and manage the multiple passwords they used, especially if they employed the coping strategy of synchronizing passwords across multiple accounts. The fact that different passwords also expired at different times was also a source of confusion, and even those who tried to update all their passwords on the schedule of the one with the shortest expiry time found it difficult to keep up. NIST’s system owners may not have intended to cause this situation, but it is the natural consequence of an environment where password policies for many applications were created in isolation from each other and may have been inherited from legacy systems.
contents.html_ja: 統一された一貫性のあるパスワードポリシーがないために、参加者が使用する複数のパスワードを作成し管理することが、それだけ難しくなりました。特に、複数のアカウント間でパスワードを同期させるという対処戦略を使っていた場合はそうでした。異なるパスワードが異なる時期に期限切れになることも、混乱の原因であり、有効期限が最も短いもののスケジュールに合わせてすべてのパスワードを更新しようとした人でさえ、それについていくことが困難だとわかりました。NIST のシステム所有者は、この状況を引き起こすつもりはなかったかもしれませんが、これは、多くのアプリケーションのパスワードポリシーが互いに独立して作成され、レガシーシステムから引き継がれた可能性のある環境の、当然の結果です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.2.4 Encourage and support the use of password managers or vaults
contents.html_ja: 7.2.4 パスワードマネージャーまたはパスワードボールトの使用を奨励し、支援する
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89: 見出し 7.2.4

contents.html: Finally, it is recommended that organizations actively support a user coping mechanism that, when practiced correctly, significantly reduces authentication burden while maintaining security: password management tools. (Individual users are also recommended to look into password managers or vaults for their personal use.) As described earlier, participants described password management tools as considerably simplifying password entry, which is especially useful for users who need to authenticate multiple times during the course of a day.
contents.html_ja: 最後に、組織が、正しく実践すれば、セキュリティを維持しながら認証の負担を大幅に減らすユーザーの対処の仕組み、すなわちパスワード管理ツールを積極的に支援することを推奨します。（個々のユーザーにも、個人用としてパスワードマネージャーまたはパスワードボールトを検討することを推奨します。）前述のように、参加者は、パスワード管理ツールがパスワードの入力を大幅に簡素化したと述べており、これは、1 日の間に複数回認証する必要があるユーザーにとって特に有用です。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.3 FUTURE DIRECTIONS
contents.html_ja: 7.3 今後の方向性
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89: 見出し 7.3

contents.html: Although there are a number of different authentication mechanisms that employ a variety of different authentication elements (including PIV cards, RSA tokens, and biometrics), password-based mechanisms are by far the most common. They were the first authentication mechanism to be used on computers, starting with timesharing systems in the 1960s [15]. Users of these systems were required to enter a password once: to log on to the computer. This required a trivial amount of time and effort and did not overly disrupt any particular primary task. The relative few individuals who used computing resources needed only one simple password, which typically only had to be changed if there was good reason to believe it had been compromised.
contents.html_ja: PIV カード、RSA トークン、生体情報など、さまざまな異なる認証要素を用いる、数多くの異なる認証の仕組みがありますが、パスワードベースの仕組みが、圧倒的に最も一般的です。これは、1960 年代のタイムシェアリングシステムに始まり、コンピュータで最初に使われた認証の仕組みでした [15]。これらのシステムのユーザーは、コンピュータにログオンするために、パスワードを 1 回入力することが求められました。これには、わずかな時間と労力しか必要とせず、特定の主要タスクを過度に中断させることもありませんでした。コンピューティングリソースを使った比較的少数の個人は、単純なパスワード 1 つだけで済み、そのパスワードは通常、危殆化したと考える十分な理由がある場合にのみ変更すればよいものでした。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89: 段落と一致

contents.html: Computing technology and the way we use it has changed radically since then. But we are still using passwords as our default method of authentication in essentially the same way: one password per technological asset. This was effective and appropriate in the days when a user would interact with, at most, a handful of password-protected assets on a daily basis. But now that most users interact with dozens of such assets – devices, applications, Web pages, networks, etc. – protecting each one with a password is no longer practical. There are simply more than most users can remember, especially with the added complication of policies that require passwords to be longer, more complex, and subject to frequent expiration.
contents.html_ja: コンピューティング技術と、それを使う方法は、それ以来、根本的に変化しました。しかし、私たちは依然として、パスワードを、本質的に同じ方法、すなわち技術的資産ごとに 1 つのパスワードという方法で、認証の既定の方法として使っています。これは、ユーザーが日常的にやり取りするパスワードで保護された資産が、せいぜい一握りだった時代には、効果的で適切でした。しかし、今では大半のユーザーが、デバイス、アプリケーション、Web ページ、ネットワークなど、数十もの資産とやり取りしているため、それぞれをパスワードで保護することは、もはや現実的ではありません。特に、パスワードをより長く、より複雑にし、頻繁な期限切れの対象とすることを求めるポリシーによって複雑さが加わっているため、ほとんどのユーザーが覚えられる数を、単純に超えています。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p89〜90: ページをまたぐ段落で全文を確認

contents.html: 7.3.1 Take a broader perspective
contents.html_ja: 7.3.1 より広い視野を持つ
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p90: 見出し 7.3.1

contents.html: Mary Theofanos and Ellen Cram Kowalczyk observed at a recent NIST Information Security and Privacy Advisory Board (ISPAB) meeting, that we have evolved from thinking “the user is the problem” to “technology is the solution”, to the realization that “the user must be part of the solution” [24]. However this holistic approach requires us to fully understand the user and embrace the considerable social science knowledge relevant to usability and computer systems. Taking a broader perspective, allows us to build usability into our security products and processes, that span the life of a system from conception through design, implementation, and evolution. Good usability, like good security takes into account the changing nature of the threat environment, changing business goals, and differences in user needs, skills, attitudes, and experience. In addition, usable security should be tailored to organizational priorities and needs.
contents.html_ja: Mary Theofanos と Ellen Cram Kowalczyk は、最近の NIST の情報セキュリティ・プライバシー諮問委員会（ISPAB）の会合で、私たちが、「ユーザーが問題である」という考えから、「技術が解決策である」という考えを経て、「ユーザーが解決策の一部でなければならない」という認識へと進化してきたと指摘しました [24]。しかし、この全体的なアプローチでは、ユーザーを十分に理解し、ユーザビリティとコンピュータシステムに関する相当量の社会科学の知識を取り入れる必要があります。より広い視野から捉えることで、構想から設計、実装、進化に至るシステムのライフサイクル全体にわたるセキュリティ製品とプロセスに、ユーザビリティを組み込むことができます。優れたユーザビリティは優れたセキュリティと同様に、脅威環境の変化する性質、変化する事業目標、およびユーザーのニーズ、スキル、態度、経験の違いを考慮に入れます。さらに、使いやすいセキュリティは、組織の優先事項とニーズに合わせて調整されるべきです。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p90: 段落と一致
contents.translation_resolve_note: 「調整されるべきです」で should を訳しており、文意も正しい。

contents.html: Authentication throughout an organization should be driven by an overall authentication strategy or approach that is driven by organizational security priorities and user needs and provides a vision for future growth. It appears in many cases that as systems are deployed that there is no overall strategy that governs the authentication mechanism offered and how it complements or prepares for the future.
contents.html_ja: 組織全体の認証は、組織のセキュリティの優先事項とユーザーのニーズに基づき、将来の成長に向けたビジョンを提供する、全体的な認証の戦略またはアプローチによって導かれるべきです。多くの場合、システムが展開される際に、提供される認証の仕組みと、それが将来をどのように補完し、あるいは準備するかを統制する全体的な戦略が存在しないように見受けられます。
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p90: 段落と一致

contents.html: 7.3.2 Establish best practices for implementing usable authentication
contents.html_ja: 7.3.2 使いやすい認証を実装するためのベストプラクティスを確立する
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p90: 見出し 7.3.2

contents.html: Essentially, usability best practices must give IT and security professionals a roadmap for understanding the context of use for whatever asset they are working with and assessing how they can implement authentication in a way that fits that context. For example, does securing a transaction require making the user authenticate, or would it be more effective to authenticate the transaction itself? Is it possible to secure a system through implicit authentication, where the system satisfies itself that this is the authorized user [2]?
contents.html_ja: 本質的に、ユーザビリティのベストプラクティスは、IT およびセキュリティの専門家に、扱うあらゆる資産の利用の文脈を理解し、その文脈に合う形で認証をどのように実装できるかを評価するための、ロードマップを提供しなければなりません。たとえば、トランザクションを保護するには、ユーザーに認証させる必要があるでしょうか。それとも、トランザクション自体を認証する方が効果的でしょうか。システムが、これが許可されたユーザーであると自ら確信する暗黙的な認証によって、システムを保護することは可能でしょうか [2]。

contents.html: Sections 5 and 6 described some methodological tools (experience graphs and prototyping with CogTool) for measuring the effect of authentication on users, as well as recommendations for improving the usability of password-based authentication; these could be considered as a basis for best practices. But that is not nearly enough. Security and IT professionals need best practices that help them apply some basic principles of social science and design. Best practices should also guide the effective development and use of the modular authentication solutions we described in the previous section.

contents.html: This study makes strong methodological contributions in identifying and measuring the impact of explicit authentication on users. The experience journey maps discussed in Sec. 5 (and shown for each participant in Appendix B) and their underlying measures can potentially be used by organizations to track and manage the effects of authentication on their customers or users. The experience journey maps, along with analyses that can be achieved through prototyping tools like CogTool, could be useful to IT and security professionals as they make security decisions that take user effort into account.

contents.html: Even without analytical tools such as the user experience journey maps and CogTool task analysis, the authors believe that usability researchers and organizations can gain valuable insights by conducting diary studies and follow-up interviews similar to those employed by this study. At a minimum, such studies are useful for collecting feedback and identifying the most widespread and persistent authentication issues within an organization. Studies with a larger number of participants than this one, would potentially reach a broader audience within an organization for an even broader perspective of the issues surrounding authentication.

contents.html: Longer-term diary studies, spanning the course of a week or more, may also be valuable. However, the data collection methods would have to be changed slightly in order to make this feasible for study participants. Expecting participants to record every single instance of authentication over a long-term period would add significantly to their authentication burden, which is the exact opposite of what we want to accomplish, and they would probably find journaling activities difficult to sustain for more than one day. One plausible variation would be to have participants record significant authentication related events (including problems) at the end of the day, while their actual authentications would be counted through some automated means. The data from a series of periodic interviews would be invaluable, although the number of interviews should be related to the length of the study period.

contents.html: This study provided a very clear picture of the average government knowledge worker’s authentication workload at NIST during the course of a typical day. While participants were using technology, any kind of technology at all, the impact of authentication was present. The study participants spent a considerable amount of time and effort on authentication each day. Participants tried very hard to cope with this workload in ways that they thought would preserve organizational security. It is important to note that they dealt with authentication not only at work, but also in their personal lives, on their computers and devices outside of the work environment. Organizations may not consider it incumbent to count users’ personal authentication workload since they cannot control it. But it is an important factor that cannot be ignored, as people cannot divide their cognitive effort: they need to be able to accommodate some personal authentication events as well as work events.
contents.html_ja: この調査は、NIST における典型的な 1 日の間の、平均的な政府のナレッジワーカーの認証の作業負荷について、非常に明確な状況を示しました。参加者が技術を使っている間は、どのような種類の技術であっても、認証の影響が存在しました。調査参加者は、毎日、認証に相当な時間と労力を費やしていました。参加者は、組織のセキュリティを維持できると考える方法で、この作業負荷に対処しようと懸命に努力しました。彼らが、職場だけでなく、私生活でも、職場環境外の自分のコンピュータやデバイスで、認証に対処していたことに注意することが重要です。組織は、ユーザーの個人的な認証の作業負荷を管理できないため、それを数えることが自らの責務だとは考えないかもしれません。しかし、それは無視できない重要な要因です。人は認知的な労力を分けられないためです。人は、業務のイベントだけでなく、個人的な認証イベントにも対応できる必要があります。

contents.html: These findings lead us to a set of recommendations, described in Sec. 7. Most importantly, the underlying assumptions about authentication must be revisited, as the human limitations of users must be respected. For NIST in particular, further implementation of SSO and incorporation of an accepted password vault or manager would help reduce the friction of authentication for NIST knowledge workers. Moreover, we believe that the findings from this study generalize to the average government knowledge worker, as the password authentication workload found here is consistent with the findings from a much larger, Department of Commerce-wide study on password related behaviors [5].
contents.html_ja: これらの調査結果は、第 7 節で説明した一連の推奨事項につながります。最も重要なのは、ユーザーの人間としての限界を尊重しなければならないため、認証に関する基礎となる前提を見直さなければならないということです。特に NIST については、SSO のさらなる実装と、承認されたパスワードボールトまたはパスワードマネージャーの導入が、NIST のナレッジワーカーの認証の摩擦を減らす助けとなるでしょう。さらに、ここで見られたパスワード認証の作業負荷は、パスワード関連の行動に関する、商務省全体のはるかに大規模な調査 [5] の結果と一致しているため、この調査の結果は、平均的な政府のナレッジワーカーに一般化できると私たちは考えています。

contents.html: APPENDIX C: CATALOG OF PARTICIPANT QUOTES ON AUTHENTICATION-RELATED FRICTION POINTS, COPING STRATEGIES, AND HABITS
contents.html_ja: 付録 C: 認証に関連する摩擦点、対処戦略、習慣に関する参加者の発言の一覧
contents.extraction_note: 原本画像と文字層で照合（Claude Opus）。原本p124: 付録Cの分類見出し（階層2）。番号・灰色の上位分類も印字どおり

contents.html: The material in this appendix comes from follow-up interviews researchers conducted with participants following the data collection period. It consists of direct quotes (and, to a lesser extent, paraphrased statements written by researchers) regarding participants’ authentication-related experiences, perceptions, and behaviors. The quotes and paraphrased statements are organized by subject category in a hierarchical format. The “top-level” categories (indicated by Roman numerals) deal with five general areas related to authentication: the entry of authentication information; the management of that information; the impact of authentication on primary tasks; authentication coping strategies; and authentication’s unintended effects on work habits. Each section is further divided into parts that “drill down” into specific concepts, actions, or topics addressed by our participants. The quotes and paraphrased themselves are italicized, bulleted items appearing under the appropriate subject category (direct quotes have quotation marks, while the paraphrased statements do not). Each quote or paraphrased statement is attributed to the participant from whom it originated by means of the participant designations (e.g., P3, P17, P22) used in this study.
contents.html_ja: この付録の内容は、データ収集期間の後に研究者が参加者に実施したフォローアップインタビューから得たものです。参加者の認証に関連する経験、認識、行動についての、直接の発言（および、より少ない程度で、研究者が書いた言い換えの記述）で構成されています。発言と言い換えの記述は、階層的な形式で、主題のカテゴリ別に整理されています。（ローマ数字で示された）「最上位」のカテゴリは、認証に関連する5つの一般的な領域を扱います。認証情報の入力、その情報の管理、認証が主要タスクに与える影響、認証への対処戦略、認証が仕事の習慣に与える意図しない影響です。各節はさらに、参加者が取り上げた具体的な概念、行動、話題を「掘り下げる」部分に分けられています。発言と言い換えの記述そのものは、該当する主題カテゴリの下に斜体の箇条書き項目として示されています（直接の発言には引用符が付き、言い換えの記述には付きません）。各発言または言い換えの記述は、この調査で用いた参加者の呼称（たとえばP3、P17、P22）によって、その発言元の参加者に帰属させています。

contents.html: “I probably mistype it at least once every day. But again, I know what it is and I just need to either slow down. It's easy to fat finger, especially on a laptop keyboard. Maybe if I had an ergonomic one I'd type better.” (P9)

contents.html: “It was really fascinating to have authentication fully in my consciousness as opposed to just kind of background and automatically happening. I think I typed – I made fewer typos. contents.html: “[T]he first time I have logged in at the airport, I guess, then I got the message, "Oh, change your password, it will expire in two days." I am thinking I am out of town; I am not changing right now. I don't want to have to deal with that. Where am I going to write it down. And then the next day it's "Password is expiring in one day." Then I was trying to change it and I got interrupted by something or something, I don't remember, I'd have to look back at exactly what happened. But it's just that fact that you have to change it so much more frequently for Time and Attendance.” (P11)
contents.html_ja: 「空港で初めてログインしたときだったと思いますが、「パスワードを変更してください。2日後に期限切れになります」というメッセージが出ました。町を離れているのだから、今は変更しない、と思いました。そんなことに対処したくありませんでした。どこに書き留めたらいいのでしょう。そして翌日には「パスワードは1日後に期限切れになります」となりました。そこで変更しようとしたのですが、何かで中断されたか何かで、覚えていません。正確に何が起きたかは、記録を振り返って確認する必要がありそうです。でも、Time and Attendanceでは、はるかに頻繁に変更しなければならないという、その事実が問題なのです。」（P11）

contents.html: “[W]hen I started getting into the WebTA thing, it just so happened that it was time to change my password and WebTA makes you change your password more frequently than the NIST general domain. And every time I have to do that, I get really frustrated because I am like why can't they always be in sync. You have to think if you are going to be the responsible person, then you have to think of different passwords for everything and it is very frustrating. So when it gets to those infrequently used passwords, then I get really irritated.“ (P11)
contents.html_ja: 「WebTA を使い始めたとき、ちょうどパスワードを変更する時期でした。WebTA は NIST の一般的なドメインよりも頻繁にパスワードの変更を求めます。そして、そのたびに、なぜいつも同期させられないのかと本当にフラストレーションを感じます。責任を持つ人になるなら、すべてのものに異なるパスワードを考えなければならず、それはとてもフラストレーションの大きいことです。ですから、使用頻度の低いパスワードになると、本当に苛立ちます。」（P11）

contents.html: “[L]ast time I needed to sign something, I don't remember if it was a travel voucher, it was something I needed to sign. So the secretary e-mails me, tells me it's ready for my signature and e-approval. I put it off because I know I don't have time to deal with the password reset, I don't have time to do that right now, I will do it at the end of the day and then it's too late because you can't call because they are not there to reset the password for you. And so this drags out over the course of maybe a week or longer and then she in the meantime has taken the time to send me another reminder e-mail, and then I feel bad because I am wasting her time. But I just couldn't get it done because I couldn't remember the thing and I didn't have the time allocated to do the whole reset thing. And I know that sounds silly, because you're like, "How long can a phone call be?" But it takes time and especially when you have to wait for them to do. […] Especially when you have to wait for them to generate the thing, and then you have to go downstairs and pick it up. I mean that's just a whole category on its own. […] Because it has rippling effects. You know, it wasn't just affecting me, it's affecting people that I am calling. […] It's affecting her trying to send me these reminder e-mails and whoever else is doing budgeting, I haven't signed for the thing yet. I mean it really has this kind of ripple in the pond effect.” (P11)
contents.html_ja: 「前回、何かに署名する必要があったとき、出張旅費の請求書だったかどうかは覚えていませんが、何か署名が必要なものでした。それで秘書から電子メールが来て、署名と電子承認の準備ができたと知らせてくれました。パスワードのリセットに対処する時間がないとわかっていたので、先送りしました。今はその時間がないので、一日の終わりにやろうと思いましたが、その時にはもう遅すぎます。パスワードをリセットしてくれる人が不在なので、電話しても連絡がつかないからです。それで、これが1週間かそれ以上にわたって長引き、その間に彼女は別のリマインダーの電子メールを送ってくれます。私は彼女の時間を無駄にしていると申し訳なく思います。でも、そのものを思い出せず、リセット全体のための時間を割り当てていなかったので、終わらせられませんでした。それがばかげて聞こえるのはわかっています。「電話ってどれくらいかかるの」と思うでしょう。でも時間がかかりますし、特に相手が対応してくれるのを待たなければならないときはそうです。[……] 特に、相手がそれを生成するのを待って、それから階下に行って受け取らなければならないときはそうです。それだけで独立した問題のカテゴリーになります。[……] 波及効果があるからです。私にだけ影響しているのではなく、私が電話をかける相手にも影響しています。[……] 彼女がリマインダーの電子メールを送ることにも、予算を扱っているほかの誰かにも影響します。私がまだその書類に署名していないからです。本当に、池に広がる波紋のような効果があります。」（P11）

contents.html: “The time cost to authenticate, if it's this automatic, non-effortful thing is minimal and I don't pay attention to it, it doesn't really frustrate me. If it is a large time cost, like me having to call and get my password reset and then you have to wait for them to generate this letter and then you have to go downstairs and pick it up, and it's like this really extended evolution. That is in a category all its own, it's very special.” (P11)

contents.html: “Once you get onto the NIST network through the secure client server, then if you change your password it can update it with the NIST servers. contents.html: “So there's the confusion of is this our BizFlow password? Is it our general realm password? Is it our Entrust password? Then they enter the password wrong. […] Most users will say, "This is my e-Approval password." But e-Approval is a combination of now two different passwords, the general realm password and the Entrust password. But people think, "My e-Approval password," which will easily get them confused.” (P3)
contents.html_ja: 「それで、これは BizFlow のパスワードなのか、一般的なレルムのパスワードなのか、Entrust のパスワードなのかという混乱があります。それで、パスワードを間違って入力します。そして、パスワードのリセットが必要だと考えますが、実際に入力しているのは Entrust のパスワードではないので、必要ありません。ですから、その点で大変な混乱です。[……] ほとんどのユーザーは、「これが私の e-Approval のパスワードです」と言うでしょう。しかし、e-Approval は、現在は 2 つの異なるパスワード、すなわち一般的なレルムのパスワードと Entrust のパスワードの組み合わせです。それなのに、人々は「私の e-Approval のパスワード」と考えるので、簡単に混乱してしまいます。」（P3）

contents.html: “Wednesday, when I recorded things, I was working from home and I was using my Mac laptop, and recently we were all forced by the NIST security policy to have the Mac centrally managed. That meant some encryption software being put on the system. Then the system times out fairly frequently and it also reboots if you leave it unattended for roughly 45 minutes or so. That added significantly to the amount of re-authentication I had to do. I have known for awhile that authentication issues have become excessively burdensome, I think. They are for everybody, I think, regardless of what you're doing, whether it's work or...“ (P21)
contents.html_ja: 「水曜日、記録をとった日は、自宅で作業していて、Mac のノートコンピュータを使っていました。最近、NIST のセキュリティポリシーによって、Mac を一元管理することを全員が強制されました。それは、システムに暗号化ソフトウェアが導入されることを意味しました。その結果、システムはかなり頻繁にタイムアウトし、約 45 分ほど放置すると再起動もします。それは、私が行わなければならない再認証の量を大幅に増やしました。しばらく前から、認証の問題が過度に負担の大きいものになっていると感じていました。仕事であれ何であれ、何をしているかにかかわらず、誰にとってもそうだと思います……」（P21）

contents.html: <sup>18</sup> This participant may be conflating “logging out” of a user account with “locking” it – the two functions do different things. “Logging out” on both Windows and OSX terminates any active processes started by the user. “Locking” a computer keeps user processes running, but they will not accept input until the computer has been unlocked. On a Mac, this option is called “sleep.” The participant was probably unfamiliar with how to “lock” a Mac. Since NIST Macs were not configured with a timed lockout until shortly before this study, the participant never had a reason to try to preemptively lock his/her computer (or, rather, put it to sleep), and logged out by accident the first time he/she tried it.
contents.html_ja: <sup>18</sup> この参加者は、ユーザーアカウントの「ログアウト」と「ロック」を混同している可能性があります。この2つの機能は異なる動作をします。Windows と OSX のどちらでも、「ログアウト」はユーザーが開始した実行中のプロセスをすべて終了させます。コンピュータを「ロック」すると、ユーザーのプロセスは実行され続けますが、コンピュータのロックが解除されるまで入力を受け付けません。Mac では、このオプションは「スリープ」と呼ばれます。この参加者は、おそらく Mac を「ロック」する方法を知らなかったのでしょう。NIST の Mac では、この調査の少し前までタイムアウトによるロックが設定されていなかったため、この参加者にはコンピュータをあらかじめロックする（あるいは、より正確にはスリープさせる）理由がなく、初めて試したときに誤ってログアウトしてしまいました。

contents.html: “One of the aspects of security is here they have fixed IP addresses. I can't plug my laptop into our wired network, even though it's a NAIS registered computer. Can't do that, because it's on the fixed IP address. And none of the printers are connected to the wireless except for that one, are connected to the wireless printer. That one's physically connected, so you can print it. I can't print on our big printers, unless I log into this one again. I have to keep two computers running. Well, that's inane. I had been keeping notes of a meeting in someone else's office, and I'm on NAIS NET. And we were like, "OK, so we can print it off." What you had to go through to print the damn thing off! Because we couldn't hook my computer up to his printer, the wireless network doesn't access printers. And we couldn't just hook, what you would do anywhere else, which is unhook it from the back of his computer and hook it into yours. […] And it wouldn't do it. You can't do any of that, which just drives me crazy. Instead, we have to eventually e-mail it.” (P2)
contents.html_ja: 「セキュリティの側面の1つですが、ここでは固定IPアドレスが使われています。NAISに登録されたコンピュータであっても、ノートコンピュータを有線ネットワークにつなぐことはできません。固定IPアドレスだからです。そして、プリンタは、あの1台を除いて無線ネットワークには接続されていません。あの1台は物理的に接続されているので、印刷できます。このコンピュータにもう一度ログインしない限り、大型プリンタでは印刷できません。コンピュータを2台動かしておかなければなりません。まったくばかげています。私は別の人のオフィスで会議のメモを取っていて、NAIS NETに接続していました。それで、「よし、これを印刷できる」となりました。あれを印刷するために、いったいどれだけの手間がかかったことか。私のコンピュータをその人のプリンタにつなげられなかったからです。無線ネットワークからはプリンタにアクセスできません。それに、ほかの場所なら普通にするように、その人のコンピュータの背面からケーブルを抜いて自分のコンピュータにつなぐこともできませんでした。[……] それでも印刷できませんでした。そうしたことが何もできず、本当に頭にきます。結局、電子メールで送ることになります。」（P2）

contents.html: “So a situation where authentication has been a real challenge and caused real problems, there's one example I can think of where I have a system that had completely failed, and I had to restore the system from a backup, a procedure that I've done a few times, works flawlessly without any problems. In this particular case there was some...just call it a bug that interfered with restoring the passwords to this device. These are root-level passwords, very low-level and basic passwords you log in to control a system, basically, the only account on this device, right? There's one account and it's super-user, super-privilege. That password had not been properly been reset, or it was...I think it was actually reset to a very, very, old password that...in hindsight it was a very, very old password, and it took me about three hours to figure out that that was the password that was in place and that something had happened in the configuration, and it restored a really old password or something like that. So that was very, very frustrating. The cost was actually high then. We had three hours, or two hours, of complete network failure of major component of our network, a major section of our network. So the cost was actually very high there, and it was all because the expected outcome of a restore didn't happen that way. […] the real cost is with all the people that are not able to use their systems and get their work done.” (P5)
contents.html_ja: 「認証が本当に難題となり、実際に問題を引き起こした状況として、思い当たる例が1つあります。システムが完全に故障し、バックアップから復元しなければなりませんでした。この手順は何度か行っており、いつも問題なく完璧に動作します。このときは、このデバイスにパスワードを復元するのを妨げる何かがありました……バグと呼んでおきましょう。これらはルートレベルのパスワード、つまりシステムを制御するためにログインするときの、ごく低レベルで基本的なパスワードです。基本的に、このデバイス上にある唯一のアカウントです。アカウントは1つだけで、それはスーパーユーザーで、非常に高い特権を持っています。そのパスワードが正しくリセットされていなかったか、あるいは……実際には、非常に古いパスワードにリセットされていたのだと思います。後から考えると、それは非常に古いパスワードでした。そのパスワードが設定されていると突き止め、構成で何かが起きて非常に古いパスワードか何かが復元されたのだと分かるまでに、約3時間かかりました。本当に、とても苛立たしいことでした。そのときの損失は実際に大きなものでした。ネットワークの主要な構成要素、つまりネットワークの主要部分が、2時間、あるいは3時間にわたり完全に停止しました。ですから、損失は非常に大きく、すべては復元によって期待どおりの結果が得られなかったことが原因でした。[……] 本当の損失は、システムを使って仕事を進められなかったすべての人々に生じました。」（P5）

So I can't even use one secure password base on all of my accounts. It's very frustrating. I manage most of my passwords by writing them down on paper.” (P7)

contents.html: “One of the aspects of security is here they have fixed IP addresses. I can't plug my laptop into our wired network, even though it's a NAIS registered computer. Can't do that, because it's on the fixed IP address. And none of the printers are connected to the wireless except for that one, are connected to the wireless printer. That one's physically connected, so you can print it. I can't print on our big printers, unless I log into this one again. I have to keep two computers running. Well, that's inane. I had been keeping notes of a meeting in someone else's office, and I'm on NAIS NET. And we were like, "OK, so we can print it off." What you had to go through to print the damn thing off! Because we couldn't hook my computer up to his printer, the wireless network doesn't access printers. And we couldn't just hook, what you would do anywhere else, which is unhook it from the back of his computer and hook it into yours. […] And it wouldn't do it. You can't do any of that, which just drives me crazy. Instead, we have to eventually e-mail it.” (P2)
contents.html_ja: 「セキュリティの側面の 1 つですが、ここでは固定 IP アドレスが使われています。NAIS に登録されたコンピュータであっても、ノートコンピュータを有線ネットワークにつなぐことはできません。固定 IP アドレスだからです。そして、プリンタはどれも無線に接続されていません。ただし、あの 1 台を除きます。あれはワイヤレスプリンタに接続されていて、物理的にもつながっているので印刷できます。このコンピュータにもう一度ログインしない限り、大型プリンタでは印刷できません。コンピュータを 2 台動かしておかなければなりません。まったくばかげています。私は別の人のオフィスで会議のメモを取っていて、NAIS NET に接続していました。「よし、印刷できるね」となりました。あれを印刷するために、どれだけ面倒な手順を踏まなければならなかったことか。私のコンピュータをその人のプリンタにつなげなかったからです。無線ネットワークからはプリンタにアクセスできません。その人のコンピュータの背面からケーブルを外して自分のコンピュータにつなぐという、ほかの場所ならできることもできませんでした。[……] それでも印刷できませんでした。そうしたことが何もできず、本当に頭にきます。結局、電子メールで送らなければなりません。」（P2）

contents.html: “It's funny, because I'll sit here and I can do my e-mail on my desktop, but most of the time, if I'm working on a document or something, I just have the Blackberry in front of me. It typically gets e-mail before I get it on my desktop. I'll just look at the e-mail on my Blackberry and keep working on whatever document I'm doing on my desktop. I'm not sure why I do it. I guess it's a convenience thing because I don't have to close the document and open up... Bring up Outlook. I find it less interruption on the work flow. [...] I don't have to interrupt the work I'm working on [...] the Blackberry is like a prescreening. I don't need to see that now. I don't need to see that. Ooh, that one I need to see it now. A lot of times I'll pop up Outlook and say, "OK, I need to see what this was," and deal with it. It is easier to respond on a big keyboard than the Blackberry. The more I'm talking about it, it's a prescreening of the e-mail to decide I don't really need to interrupt what I'm doing.” (P15)
contents.html_ja: 「おかしなことですが、ここに座ってデスクトップで電子メールを扱えるのに、たいてい文書か何かを作成しているときは、目の前にBlackberryを置いています。電子メールは通常、デスクトップに届くより先にBlackberryに届きます。Blackberryでメールを見るだけにして、デスクトップで作業中の文書を続けます。なぜそうするのかはわかりません。文書を閉じてOutlookを開く必要がないので、便利だからだと思います。作業の流れを中断することが少ないと感じます。[……] 作業中の仕事を中断しなくて済みます。[……] Blackberryはメールを事前に選別する手段のようなものです。「これは今見る必要はない。これも見る必要はない。ああ、これは今見る必要がある」と判断します。多くの場合、Outlookを立ち上げて、「よし、これは何だったか確認しよう」と言って対処します。Blackberryよりも大きなキーボードのほうが返信しやすいです。話しているうちに、これは自分がしていることを本当に中断する必要があるかどうかを判断するための、メールの事前選別なのだと思えてきました。」（P15）

contents.html: “[L]ast time I needed to sign something, I don't remember if it was a travel voucher, it was something I needed to sign. So the secretary e-mails me, tells me it's ready for my signature and e-approval. I put it off because I know I don't have time to deal with the password reset, I don't have time to do that right now, I will do it at the end of the day and then it's too late because you can't call because they are not there to reset the password for you. And so this drags out over the course of maybe a week or longer and then she in the meantime has taken the time to send me another reminder e-mail, and then I feel bad because I am wasting her time. But I just couldn't get it done because I couldn't remember the thing and I didn't have the time allocated to do the whole reset thing. And I know that sounds silly, because you're like, "How long can a phone call be?" But it takes time and especially when you have to wait for them to do. […] Especially when you have to wait for them to generate the thing, and then you have to go downstairs and pick it up. I mean that's just a whole category on its own. […] Because it has rippling effects. You know, it wasn't just affecting me, it's affecting people that I am calling. […] It's affecting her trying to send me these reminder e-mails and whoever else is doing budgeting, I haven't signed for the thing yet. I mean it really has this kind of ripple in the pond effect.” (P11)
contents.html_ja: 「前回、何かに署名する必要があったとき、出張旅費の精算書だったかは覚えていませんが、とにかく署名が必要なものでした。それで秘書から電子メールが来て、署名と電子承認をしてもらう準備ができたと知らせてくれました。パスワードのリセットに対処する時間がないとわかっていたので、先送りしました。今はその時間がないから、一日の終わりにやろうと思いましたが、その時にはもう遅すぎます。パスワードをリセットしてもらうために電話しても、担当者がもういないからです。それで、1週間かそれ以上にわたって長引き、その間に彼女はわざわざ別のリマインダーの電子メールを送ってくれました。私は彼女の時間を無駄にしていると申し訳なく思います。でも、パスワードを思い出せず、リセット作業全体のための時間も割り当てていなかったので、終わらせられませんでした。ばかげて聞こえるのはわかっています。「電話ってどれだけ時間がかかるの」と思うでしょう。でも時間がかかります。特に、相手が対応してくれるのを待たなければならない場合はそうです。[……] 特に、相手がそれを生成してくれるのを待って、それから階下に行って受け取らなければならない場合はそうです。それだけでひとつの大きな問題です。[……] 波及効果があるからです。私だけでなく、私が電話をかけている人たちにも影響します。[……] 彼女がリマインダーの電子メールを送ろうとすることにも影響しますし、予算を扱っているほかの人にも影響します。私がまだその書類に署名していないからです。本当に、池に広がる波紋のような影響があります。」（P11）

contents.html: “Things get put off until when it's, "OK, I have a block of time. […] especially if it's something that wasn't actually due. It's after hours. You've already put in your nine hours or however many hours you're doing and then you think of something of home, it definitely is less likely that you're going to get online to actually do that thing that you're thinking of. contents.html: “[W]hen I'm at home, if I'm downstairs, and even if I have my work laptop there which I do. I have a property password, if I have my work laptop there and I think, "Oh, I need to send this e-mail," if I have to go upstairs into my office and get my RSA token, I am likely to just scribble a note on a piece of paper and remember it the next day, hopefully. So, it definitely changes my behavior. That's a good question. I had not thought of that. Same thing, like it makes me less likely to, if I'm at the airport and I close my laptop to go to the restroom or whatever, and I have 15 minutes before the plane's going to board or 10 minutes or something like that, if I have to re-authenticate and dig out that RSA token, again, then it'll make me less likely to take advantage of just a few minutes because it's that, again that kind of level of effort. […] I mean if there's something I have to get done, then of course, I will do it. But, as far as, "Oh, let me just taking advantage of every last second," you're less likely to do that because there's a cost associated with taking advantage of that time. […] We know people are sensitive to small, local costs and when I hear myself describing the fact that, oh, well me going upstairs to get the thing is going to prevent me from doing one e-mail, it sounds kind of silly, but that's what happens.” (P11)
contents.html_ja: 「自宅にいて階下にいるとき、仕事用のノートコンピュータもそこにあります。実際、そこに置いてあります。私は固有のパスワードを持っています。仕事用のノートコンピュータがそこにあって、「ああ、このメールを送らなきゃ」と思っても、2階の書斎に行ってRSAトークンを取ってこなければならないなら、紙切れにメモを走り書きして、できれば翌日まで覚えておこうとしがちです。ですから、間違いなく私の行動は変わります。いい質問です。それは考えていませんでした。同じことで、たとえば空港でノートコンピュータを閉じてトイレなどに行き、飛行機の搭乗まで15分とか10分とかある場合に、再認証してRSAトークンを取り出さなければならないなら、またしてもその程度の手間がかかるため、ほんの数分を活用する可能性が低くなります。[……] やらなければならないことがあれば、もちろんやります。でも、「ああ、最後の1秒まで活用しよう」という点では、その時間を活用するためにコストがかかるので、そうする可能性は低くなります。[……] 人は局所的な小さなコストに敏感です。2階にそれを取りに行くせいでメールを1通書かずに済ませてしまう、と自分で説明しているのを聞くと、ちょっとばかげて聞こえますが、実際にそうなるのです。」（P11）

contents.html: “Well, let's say I'm working on a Word document and I have to refer to somebody's e-mail just to see one of their comments or an attachment of something I sent myself or somebody sent me. contents.html_ja: 「ええと、Word文書を作成していて、誰かのコメントを見るためだけに、あるいは自分が送った、または誰かが私に送ってきたものの添付ファイルを見るためだけに、誰かの電子メールを参照しなければならないとします。本当に5分間、作業を止めなければなりません。そして、何かで調子が出ているときは、……。[……] ええ。すべてが台無しになります。ですから、手を止めて、これをしに行って、戻ってきて、それから仕事の流れを取り戻そうとするよりも、そのまま続けます。後回しにして、後で戻ってくるかもしれません。[……] そうして電子メールを確認する動機が生じるのを待っていると、そのたびに、おそらくもっと早い返信を望んでいた人たちからの電子メールが5、6通届いています。」（P19）

contents.html: “For the e-mail, when I was at home, if I don't do anything on the Web page for five minutes or 10 minutes, it will log me out automatically. contents.html_ja: 「電子メールについては、自宅にいるとき、Webページで5分か10分何もしないと、自動的にログアウトされます。それは煩わしいことがあります。ブラウザを閉じて、もう一度開き、RSAキーを使い、最初から正しくできることを願わなければならないからです。それを1日のうちに15回や20回することもあります。再ログインにうんざりして、電子メールを確認するのをやめてしまうことがよくあります。20分ごとではなく、3、4時間に1回くらいにするかもしれません。」（P19）

contents.html: “Respondent: And I just work away, and I have to consciously remember to check e-mail. contents.html: “[I]t's very difficult to do real collaborative work with anyone who is not a NIST employee. I have research collaborations with people in other institutions, but it is just extremely difficult to share files with them, to transfer software you're writing, and that sort of thing. To me, the way that security impacts work is not that I waste a few seconds typing in a password, but it is these things that you just can't do because of the limitations of security policy. […] I can think of cases when I have thought it would be really nice to include some person at another university on a software development project, but then I realize it is going to be such a tremendous pain to organize that.” (P6)

contents.html: Two models based on the GOMS-KLM technique were developed to model a login task similar to one NIST employees execute. The first model was developed by a member of the research team by manually modeling the task using the prescribed GOMS-KLM technique. For this model, the researchers broke the task of logging in to an e-mail app down to its most basic elements as prescribed by GOMS-KLM. GOMS-KLM includes standard durations (in seconds) for each of these actions, which were used in the task breakdown for this model. Table 17 shows an example of a GOMS-KLM sequence for the manual login, with each action and its associated time.
contents.html_ja: NIST の職員が行うものに似たログインタスクをモデル化するために、GOMS-KLM の手法に基づく 2 つのモデルが開発されました。最初のモデルは、研究チームのメンバーが、規定された GOMS-KLM の手法を用いてタスクを手動でモデル化することで開発しました。このモデルのために、研究者は、電子メールアプリへのログインのタスクを、GOMS-KLM が規定するとおり、最も基本的な要素に分解しました。GOMS-KLM には、これらの各動作の標準的な所要時間（秒単位）が含まれており、このモデルのタスクの分解に使用されました。表 17 は、手動でのログインの GOMS-KLM の手順の例を、各動作とそれに関連する時間とともに示します。

contents.html: For the second model, the research team used CogTool, a prototyping tool that predicts the amount of time required for a skilled user of an interface to perform a particular task based on data provided to the tool. The team performed the actions necessary to log into the selected e-mail app (manually and with LastPass) and took a screenshot at each step. This sequence of screenshots was then entered into CogTool, along with specifications for the buttons and fields used for interactions at each stage (e.g., the number of characters to be typed into a certain field). CogTool then assigned cognitive and physical components of the task based on the screenshots and information provided. While it used standardized GOMS-KLM durations for each task as a baseline, it also calculated its own times where possible. These calculations, which were based on Fitts’ Law [8], took into account the distance to and size of the target object users needed to click to complete an activity. Figure 17 below shows CogTool’s script for the login task. CogTool developers assert that CogTool is at least as accurate as GOMS-KLM-only models, and perhaps more so [11].
contents.html_ja: 2 つ目のモデルでは、研究チームは、ツールに与えられたデータに基づいて、インタフェースに習熟したユーザーが特定のタスクを実行するのに必要な時間を予測するプロトタイピングツールである CogTool を使いました。チームは、選択した電子メールアプリにログインするために必要な操作を（手動で、および LastPass を使って）実行し、各手順でスクリーンショットを撮りました。次に、この一連のスクリーンショットを、各段階の操作で使うボタンや欄の仕様（たとえば、特定の欄に入力する文字数）とともに CogTool に入力しました。CogTool はその後、スクリーンショットと与えられた情報に基づいて、タスクの認知的および身体的な構成要素を割り当てました。各タスクの標準化された GOMS-KLM の所要時間を基準として使用し、可能な場合には独自の時間も計算しました。これらの計算は Fitts の法則 [8] に基づいており、活動を完了するためにユーザーがクリックする必要のある対象物までの距離と対象物の大きさを考慮に入れました。下の図 17 は、ログインタスクの CogTool のスクリプトを示します。CogTool の開発者は、CogTool が GOMS-KLM のみのモデルと少なくとも同程度に正確であり、おそらくそれ以上に正確であると主張しています [11]。

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The purpose of authentication is to ensure that only authorized individuals have access to a particular resource or physical area. To authenticate and prove their “right to access,” a person must essentially prove that they are who they claim to be (i.e., an authorized individual) by presenting elements such as ID badges, fingerprints, personal identification numbers (PINs) or – very often – a username and password. For users of information technology, authentication is an inescapable fact of daily life – and it affects them in ways that are still poorly understood.

In order to better understand users’ authentication-related perceptions and behaviors, we conducted a two-part study with 25 NIST employees. In the first part of the study, we instructed our participants to record all the authentication events they encountered over a 24-hour period (in the workplace and, if they so chose, at home) using forms we provided. The second part of the study consisted of individual follow-up interviews regarding participants’ experiences with authentication.
Our study was designed to answer the following questions:
Where does authentication fit into the daily activities people carry out?
What characteristics of authentication may interfere with the primary activity that authentication is supposed to enable? What are the friction points?
How do people add up the cumulative costs of authenticating multiple times each day, and how do they balance them against their own perceived security needs?
How do people perceive the costs of performing security tasks (particularly authentication tasks) in comparison with the benefits of performing those tasks?

We found that our participants were confused about what “authentication” actually meant. For example, one participant erroneously recorded unlocking his car with his remote key fob as an authentication event. Conversely, some participants did not record showing their ID badge to a guard before entering the NIST campus (although most did). Our participants recorded an average of 23 authentication events each during the study period. Since many participants did not record authentication events outside of work, we suspect that the actual number is higher. In interviews, participants indicated that they were frustrated by the sheer number of authentication tasks they had to perform every day – especially those they had to perform repeatedly, such as unlocking work computers that auto-locked after 15 minutes. In addition, while participants were understandably frustrated by problems that interfered with the successful completion of authentication tasks, they were also frustrated by tasks that were particularly complex and/or time-consuming, even when they did not encounter problems. Participants also found it particularly effortful to manage a variety of passwords for multiple resources, especially since those passwords were often governed by different policies.

Although our participants valued organizational security and understood the benefits of authentication with regard to security, these benefits were often overshadowed by the day-to-day costs of using and managing multiple authentication elements. For that reason, many of our participants adopted behaviors to help them cope with or avoid authentication, without (from their perspective) compromising organizational security. Coping strategies included synchronizing passwords across multiple IT resources; employing password creation schemas; keeping password notes in a secure place; and employing password vaults or managers. Avoidance usually meant giving up on performing certain “extra” activities (e.g., doing additional work from home) because the cost of authenticating to do so seemed greater than the potential benefit of the activity.

Our participants are not unique in being impacted by authentication. “Password fatigue” is, in fact, a very common problem [1][13]. Expecting users to simply adapt to an excessive authentication workload is not realistic. But from the user’s perspective, what is excessive? In any case, if our participants’ coping and avoidance strategies are any indication, the ways in which users adapt may not be desirable from an organizational perspective. Rather than trying to force users to adapt to authentication, organizations, security experts, developers, and engineers must find ways to make authentication adapt to users – in other words, to make it more usable.

Ultimately, making authentication more usable will take time. Further research is needed on how authentication affects users and the habits they develop to cope with those effects. This kind of research is essential for developing more usable, context-sensitive authentication solutions that will keep interference with users’ primary tasks to an absolute minimum. Finally, there is a need for best practices aimed at designing and implementing more usable authentication.

Until then, organizations can take steps to reduce the burden of authentication on their employees, and other users of these systems, which will improve both security and productivity. This study indicates that users prefer single sign-on (SSO) authentication; another option is standardizing password policies throughout the organization, which will make authentication elements easier for users to manage. Finally, organizations can encourage and support authentication coping mechanisms such as the use of password manager or vault applications on computers and mobile electronic devices.
1 INTRODUCTION

Users must interact with a variety of applications and systems over the course of a day, in both their professional and personal lives. Each application and system has its own set of security policies and measures. Even different systems within the same organization – say, a single company or governmental agency – tend to have separate (and sometimes conflicting) security policies that are effectively “unaware” of each other. Each policy is narrowly focused on the system or application to which it directly applies, rather than the broader technological and policy environment in which the system exists.

Fragmented security policies are one reason why workers have to manage multiple passwords – between 5 and 15, according to some researchers in the usability field [1][5][9][10]. In addition, those passwords may be governed by different and even mutually exclusive password policies. One requires a password 8 characters long, while another requires a password at least 12 characters long; one mandates that the password include special characters, while another forbids them; and one expires every six weeks while another expires every ninety days. In addition to the challenges of password management, users must handle the cumulative impact imposed by the need to authenticate multiple times per day [5].

In theory, authentication is supposed to enable users to perform their primary tasks (e.g., research, financial management) in a secure way. But from a user’s perspective, authentication often interferes with the performance of primary tasks. Beautement et al. refer to this kind of interference as “friction,” a term we use in this report [5].1

Users have developed various coping strategies for minimizing or avoiding the friction and burden associated with managing and using their portfolios of user IDs and passwords or personal identification numbers (PINs). Many try to use the same password (or different versions of the same password) across different systems [10]. Others use memory aids or technological assistants such as password management software for computers and mobile electronic devices.

The research team was interested in these coping strategies and the “friction points” that prompt people to use them. More broadly, we wanted to address a pressing research need by gathering data for user-centered models of how people interact with security as part of their daily life, as empirical research in that area is currently lacking.
Specifically, this study was designed to answer the following research questions:
Where does authentication fit into the daily activities people carry out?
1 Sec. 2.3 and Sec. 2.4 contain more detailed explanations of enabling tasks, primary tasks, and friction.
What characteristics of authentication cause friction with the primary activity that authentication is supposed to enable? What are the friction points?
How do people perceive the cumulative costs of performing authentication tasks for the systems and applications they use, and how do they balance them against their own perceived security needs?
How do people perceive the costs of performing security tasks (particularly authentication tasks) in comparison with the benefits of performing those tasks?

The research team considered a few different factors in this study. A first objective was to develop an estimate of how many times in a typical day federal government knowledge workers2 authenticate – in other words, prove who they are to persons or systems. To do this, participants were asked to record the “authentication events” they encountered during a typical workday in a diary form provided by the team (shown in Appendix A). It was anticipated that by examining users’ security compliance from this angle, rather than focusing on the number of user IDs and passwords individuals maintain, some insights about usable security that have not been revealed by prior research could be obtained.

Second, the study examined instances in which participants reported situations that delayed or prevented successful completion of the authentication process, in order to identify circumstances attributed to delays and problems, e.g., friction. Finally, we investigated the factors that contributed to frustration, friction, and the use of coping strategies associated with daily use of authentication. Following the recording of authentication events, we conducted an interview with each the participant to examine these issues.

This report presents when, where, and how participants authenticated during the study period, as well the issues they encountered. Based on the findings, we quantified and developed a preliminary visual model of task disruption, success (or failure), and frustration – factors contributing to impact on the user. These factors include the mental and physical workload associated with recalling authentication elements such as passwords and PINs and the disruption that failure to recall those elements causes to the user’s activity.

Additionally, we identify and discuss the friction points of authentication that participants reported. We also relate and discuss participants’ observations about organizational security from their perspective as it relates to authentication, as well their coping mechanisms to manage the impact of authentication requirements. Insights and recommendations related to usable security were also derived from the findings.

2 BACKGROUND
This section presents key terms used in this study:
Authentication (including authentication factors)
Usability
Enabling tasks and primary tasks
Friction
Compliance budget
Password fatigue

The definitions of these terms are given below, as well as, a description of the general IT and authentication environment within NIST and how that environment affects the way authentication mechanisms are implemented and used there – important considerations for this study, since all of the participants were NIST employees.
2.1 AUTHENTICATION

The purpose of authentication is to ensure that only authorized individuals have access to a particular resource: that resource can be a system, application, database, or even a physical area. In essence, authentication requires that a person prove that they are who they claim to be, i.e., an authorized individual, using a set of authentication elements that employ some combination of the following three factors:
Something you have – a physical token such as a smart card or ID
Something you are – biometrics such as fingerprints or a facial image
Something you know – a password, code, or PIN

While there are a variety of authentication mechanisms currently in use, the one that will perhaps be most familiar to people is the combination of a user ID and password (something you know). Displaying a picture ID to a guard or holding a passcard to a reader in order to unlock a door are also common forms of authentication (something you have). One form that is becoming more and more common is a multi-factor authentication (MFA) mechanism involving a smartcard and PIN (something you have, something you know).
2.2 USABILITY

Mary Ellen Zurko and Richard T. Simon coined the term “user-centered security” in a research paper in 1996. In their paper, they described the usability lessons they had learned from their work on a user-centered rules-based authorization engine. One of their key observations was that because “security mechanisms need to be appropriately used to maintain their effectiveness…. Mechanisms and models that are confusing to the user

5 will be misused.” Not misused maliciously, in the classic sense, but unintentionally. Zurko and Simon strongly recommended that secure systems should be designed and tested for usability in order to reduce the potential for confusion and, by extension, inadvertent misuse [29].

A few years later, in 1999, Alma Whitten and Doug Tygar published the results of a usability study on Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) 5.0, a program that provides cryptographic privacy and authentication for e-mail and other online communication. In their paper, they presented the following criteria for usability:

“Security software is usable if the people who are expected to use it: (1) Are reliably made aware of the security tasks they need to perform. (2) Are able to figure out how to successfully perform those tasks. (3) Don’t make dangerous errors. (4) Are sufficiently comfortable with the interface to continue using it.” [27].
2.3 ENABLING TASKS AND PRIMARY TASKS

Authentication is something that users do on the way to some other activity – for example, logging into an e-mail application in order to send a message to a co-worker. Sending the e-mail is the primary task, while logging into the application in order to do so is the secondary task that enables it. Or, as usability researchers Dirk Weirich and Martina Angela Sasse put it:
“In most cases, authentication to a system is an enabling task, which means it creates an overhead for the user, who is using that system as a tool to achieve a primary, real-world task.” [26]

In some cases the enabling task of authentication can be transparent: it fits into the flow of the user’s primary task or happens automatically, so the user does not notice it. But in the overwhelming majority of cases, authentication is explicit – a specific set of actions that the user must take before proceeding. It is something the user must do before engaging in something he or she wants to do.
2.4 FRICTION
In a report on a study examining the factors that influence users’ compliance (or non-compliance) with organizational security requirements, Beautement et al. explained that:

“Employees focus on completing their primary (production) tasks, and the behaviour required by the security (enabling) tasks often presents an obstacle on the shortest path to the primary goal. This misalignment introduces friction between security and business processes into the organizational system, and it is this friction that is at the heart of individual compliance issues.” [5]

In other words, friction occurs when security tasks interrupt the user on his or her way to completing a primary task. Because of this friction, users must spend additional time and effort to accomplish their primary goals.
2.5 THE COMPLIANCE BUDGET

Because of the friction inherent in security tasks, as described in Sec. 2.4, users often perceive these tasks as an obstacle to engaging in and completing their primary tasks. More than that, they see little if any return on the investment of time and effort that they put into security tasks. As Beautement et al. explain, users have a limited tolerance for the disruption related to security tasks:

“There is a limit to the amount of effort individuals are prepared to expend on security measures that do not obviously contribute to their key production tasks, and this extra non-productive effort required accumulates until a limit is reached. We have named this limit the Compliance Budget… The limit of the Compliance Budget is referred to as the compliance threshold; this being the point at which the individual no longer has the will to comply with official requirements.” [5]

For users, cost/benefit calculations related to the compliance budget are largely non-quantified, just like most of the cost/benefit calculations humans perform as they make decisions on a daily basis – for example, determining the importance and urgency of individual tasks when prioritizing the tasks that might be accomplished in a given timeframe. Users cannot quantify their compliance budget. But they are aware that security requirements and security tasks cause accumulated fatigue over time.
2.6 PASSWORD FATIGUE

Password fatigue, also referred to as authentication fatigue, is conceptually related to the compliance budget and compliance threshold: it is a nearly perpetual state of stress and exhaustion experienced by technology users who are overwhelmed by authentication-related demands on their time, energy, and memory [13]. Martina Angela Sasse and Angela Adams point out that this situation is exacerbated by organizational IT departments that try to address what they see as the problem of “inherently insecure” users by escalating the number and stringency of security mechanisms and policies those users must deal with [1].

“Password fatigue” is a common term in the security and IT industries, often cited as the reason why many users – even if they are relatively security-conscious – engage in behaviors that compromise the security of the systems they use, e.g., creating passwords that are easy to guess or to compromise with password-cracking software. Another possible effect of password fatigue is changing one’s work habits to reduce or avoid authentication in a way that does not compromise security, but does have adverse effects on one’s productivity.
2.7 IT AND AUTHENTICATION AT NIST

At NIST, many and varied applications and software systems3 are required to perform the business of the organization. These applications and systems may be administered by agencies and organizations outside of NIST, e.g., other government agencies or standards bodies; and as a consequence NIST does not have control over their authentication configuration. Other systems are administered by the NIST IT system support staff, while still other (often more specialized) systems and applications may be managed by staff associated with the individual projects that make use of those applications. Users at NIST interact with multiple applications each day to do their work, each of which requires authentication. The authentication methods associated with these applications include: user ID and password, smartcard and PIN, remote token combined with smartcard and PIN, and picture ID.

As in many other organizations, the most common authentication mechanism used for logical access (i.e., access to a system or application) employs a user ID and password. Logins for a number of mission-critical applications and systems within the NIST domain are consolidated using a single sign-on (SSO) solution – for example, NIST’s domain services automatically log users into e-mail and calendar clients as well as other applications. However, Windows and OSX user profile passwords are not part of the SSO solution, nor are the passwords used for hard disk encryption on laptops. Fortunately these are all governed by the same password policy. Additionally, authentication elements for a number of other applications used at NIST – such as applications managed by the Department of Commerce – are not managed through SSO, and their password policies vary.

Some applications and systems also support smartcard-based authentication. All NIST employees have a Personal Identity Verification (PIV) smartcard with an associated 6-8 digit PIN. At the time of this writing, a relatively small number of employees use this method on a regular basis, in part because not all employees are “PIV-enabled,” i.e., they do not have the requisite card reader and middleware or operating system. Even employees who use smartcard authentication almost exclusively must still manage their NIST domain password, which expires every ninety days.

Logging into the NIST virtual private network (VPN) from off campus requires not only a user ID and password (or PIV card and PIN), but also a six-digit code from a NIST-issued RSA token, which changes every sixty seconds. To authenticate, users must enter their user ID, PIN and the RSA code, then their user ID and password. It takes a few seconds for the system to process each set of authentication elements once they are submitted, and if the RSA code expires before the authentication process is completed, the user will have to authenticate again.
